content: On the topic of equation numbering, I'm wondering why we didn't list the other trivial equations of the form w = w (like xx = xx). What was the thought process behind disregarding those equations? Was it just that they were so obviously equivalent to x=x that we ignored them?
Yeah, basically the idea was to work modulo "trivial" equivalences.

It is certainly too late for me to raise this observation, but it seems like this type of triviality is a bit different than those coming from the symmetry of the equality symbol or the renaming of variables. Partly because there are other equivalences that seems just as trivial (such as "every rule that has x on one side and an expression without x on the other is equivalent to x=y"), but if we start allowing these types of equivalences it becomes a question of what sort of metric we put on "trivial".

In other words, I could see later enumerations validly saying that x=x and xx=xx are different identities, even if they are (easily seen to be) equivalent, and thus use a different numbering than us.

Obviously I don't think we should change anything to the equation numbering at this late stage. And I hope that people can use the same numbering for magma equations to avoid confusion in the literature.

The numbering makes the following sense. If you have an equation of the form f(x,y,...) = g(x,y,...) = h(x,y,...), then the order of f,g,h does not matter, and any duplicates can be freely added or deleted, without knowing any details about f,g,h, not even what operations are involved, or what variables. For instance x=y(xy)=x should just be x=y(xy), and in that sense x=x=x is the same as x=x is the same as the empty equation that states no equality at all. All tautological equations reduce to such an empty equation so it makes sense to only have one empty equation.
I guess xx=xx does follow from reflexivity of equality. So, in that sense, it does follow from a basic fact about the constituent parts of expressions. Fair enough.

Similar to Bruno, I don't think we should change the numbering for our project at this late stage. But here are some additional thoughts.

Under our counting, we defined two equations to be numbered equivalently if we can pass back and forth between them using a sequence of (1) renaming variables (keeping distinct variables distinct), (2) using symmetry of equality, and (3) using reflexivity of equality.

An even more parsimonious numbering would have been to use logical equivalence. However, there is no algorithm to decide when two equations imply each other, so such a numbering would be a bad idea. Having a computable numbering is quite beneficial.

That said, looking our list of three conditions, it isn't clear why we didn't include "(4) using transitivity of equality." It remains (easily) computable to check which expressions are equal in the transitive closure of variable renamings (under symmetry and reflexivity of equality).

If we had added that rule (4), some of the obviously equivalent equations would have been given the same number. For example, consider the rules (A) xy=yz and (B) xy=zw.

From (A) and a simple renaming, we get yz=zw. From transitivity we get (B). Conversely, from (B) and two simple renamings, we get xy=uw and uw=yz. Hence from transitivity we get (A). Thus, (A) and (B) give the same equation in the transitive closure of variable renamings.

I think this transitive closure can only give equivalences between equations f(...)=g(...) whose left and right-hand side are obtained from each other by a relabeling (and in particular have the same shape). Otherwise transitivity can only be applied to f(args1)=g(args2)=f(args3)=g(args4) etc, with alternating f and g. The relabeling between f(args1) and f(args3) can only concern variables that do not appear in g(args2). Thus, f(args1)=g(args4) and other results of an odd number of equalities is simply the same equation we started with (up to relabeling), while f(args1)=f(args3) and other results of an even number of equalities cannot have the original equation in its transitive closure.

Concerning equations which may have non-trivial transitive closure, do you see how to count the number of equations that are distinct in this sense? One feature of our numbering is that it is possible to determine efficiently the number of equations of each order (in terms of Catalan and Bell numbers) and even the id of a given equation.

@Bruno Le Floch Yes, I believe that this transitive closure can easily be described.

First, it is trivial unless (as you noted) the right side can be obtained from the left side by a relabeling. Such a relabeling puts the letters into groups of two types: those that cycle, and those that don't.

For example, consider (x(yz))((xw)(u(vv)))=(z(yx))((zu)(v(rr))). The right side can be obtained from the left side by the renaming x->z, y->y, z->x, w->u, u->v, v->r. The letter y belongs to a 1-cycle. The letters x,z belong to a 2-cycle. And the letters w,u,v,r do not belong to a cycle.

Second, for all the letters not in a cycle, we can replace those on the right side by letters completely disjoint from those on the left (by repeated replacement, with enough replacements so that the letters in the cycle parts have all performed the needed number of turns to match the original equation).

So, continuing our example from before, the equation is equivalent to (x(yz))((xw)(u(vv)))=(z(yx))((zr)(s(tt))).

I would guess that counting these sorts of equivalences should definitely be doable.
